prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology and active form of glucagon-like peptide-1 that enabled incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: GLP-1 is the clearest unbroken line on the shortlist from a basic hormone discovery (proglucagon processing, the incretin effect, the active peptide and its actions) to therapies that have changed the care of type 2 diabetes and obesity, now with cardiovascular and renal benefit in large independent outcome trials. All six of us ranked it first or second, which I take as a sign that the discovery is clear, not as a substitute for scientific argument. The originality, the patient impact and the maturity of the evidence are all strong, and recognition is timely, arguably overdue. Holst and Drucker are the unambiguous core, and a physiology-centred prize with Mojsov for identifying the active peptide gives a coherent three-person allocation.
statement.case_against: The credit problem is real. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) form is contested against Habener and colleagues, who are not on the credited list, and I cannot settle that from the supplied text. Excluding Knudsen means the prize rewards the physiology and leaves out the person most responsible for the long-acting analogues that actually reached patients, which some will see as an incomplete account of why these drugs work as medicines. Safety and neuropsychiatric effects of very broad obesity use are still accruing, though that does not undercut the discovery.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranks GLP-1 first with Holst, Drucker and Knudsen, treating the unbroken line from physiology to long-acting liraglutide and semaglutide as the central achievement, and flags Mojsov as a credit-allocation problem.
responses.response: I proposed the same trio at opening and have moved away from it after reading the others. Knudsen's work was decisive for the drugs, but it is industrial development of a mechanism that others had already established, and the prize is for a discovery. Holst and Drucker are certain, so the third slot is where we disagree. I now favour Mojsov for identifying the active peptide, while accepting that her priority against Habener is unresolved and that this is a genuine qualification of my position. Knudsen's omission should be visible in the citation wording about enabling therapy.

responses.point: Sandberg ranks the unfolded protein response (Walter and Mori) first as a mechanistically complete, original pathway with wide relevance to proteostasis, neurodegeneration and cancer, and places GLP-1 second.
responses.response: I agree that UPR is a conceptually elegant, well-attributed two-person discovery, and the clean allocation is a real advantage over GLP-1. Where I differ is on consequence for human disease: the link to medicine is more indirect, and clinical translation of UPR modulation is still early, whereas GLP-1 has a demonstrated effect on large patient populations. I would not call UPR premature, and if GLP-1 stalls on credit it is a credible alternative, but I would not place it ahead of GLP-1 this year.

responses.point: Perlmann ranks BCL-2 (Cory, Adams, Vaux) third on the grounds that it founded the control of apoptosis in cancer and led to venetoclax, while noting the overlap with the 2002 apoptosis prize.
responses.response: BCL-2 is a solid cancer-biology discovery with real translational validation through venetoclax, but I weigh the 2002 apoptosis prize heavily, and the four-name credit plus uncredited work on the t(14;18) translocation make allocation harder than for the leading candidates. I ranked it eighth and would keep it there. I do agree with Perlmann's point that Mojsov, Drucker and Holst are the most defensible trio from the credited names, which supports my move on that third slot.

responses.point: Linnarsson ranks optogenetics second for its enabling effect across neuroscience and emerging retinal therapy, but concedes that the six-name credit forces a contentious choice of three.
responses.response: Optogenetics is a genuinely transformative method, but I share his concern about the six names, and I would add that a tool without established clinical consequence fits the medicine criteria less well than a therapy-defining discovery. Any trio leaves out Bamberg, Boyden or Hegemann, and I do not think the committee can resolve that fairly this year. I therefore keep it below the immunology candidates, though I recognise a neuroscientist will weigh the research impact more heavily than I do.

uncertainties: Priority for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide (Mojsov versus Habener and colleagues) cannot be settled from the supplied evidence.
Whether the committee wants the prize to include industrial drug development (Knudsen) or to stay with physiology.
If GLP-1 is awarded, whether CAR-T or cGAS-STING is the better candidate to hold for a later year given attribution and maturity.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for the shortlisted candidates. My field is autoimmunity and I work on type I interferon biology, so I have scientific interest in cGAS-STING and CAR-T, but I have no documented personal or institutional tie to any credited name.
